docs.title: User Guide
docs.text:
Smart AutoSorter AI Pro organizes a folder of documents into a generated folder tree. You can drive it from the full-screen terminal interface (TUI) or from the command line, and every run can be undone.

The examples below use smart-autosorter. When running from a source checkout, prefix each command with uv run.

docs.title: First Run and AI Consent
docs.text:
On first launch the Privacy & Data Setup Wizard asks whether you allow the optional AI model download: a one-time, roughly 80 MB embedding model from Hugging Face.

Declining is fine. Sorting still works offline using TF-IDF keyword clustering (see Offline Mode).

docs.title: From the command line
docs.text:
• Grant consent and download the model: 
    smart-autosorter --accept-ai-consent
  • Decline and stay fully offline: 
    smart-autosorter --decline-ai-consent
  • In scripts or other non-interactive environments, add --non-interactive (or --skip-wizard) so no dialog waits for input: 
    smart-autosorter --accept-ai-consent --non-interactive

docs.title: In the terminal interface
docs.text:
The wizard opens automatically on first launch of smart-autosorter: 1. Use [Tab] / [Shift+Tab] to move between the AI Consent switch and the buttons. 2. Press [Space] or [Enter] on the switch to toggle consent. 3. Highlight Finish & Save and press [Enter].

Reopen the wizard any time with [Ctrl+W].

docs.title: In the terminal interface
docs.text:
1. Start the app with smart-autosorter (or smart-autosorter --tui).
  2. Press [Ctrl+B] to choose a folder, then [Ctrl+S] to scan it. The proposed folder tree appears; nothing has moved yet.
  3. Review the plan. [Ctrl+F] searches the tree, [Space] checks items, [Ctrl+L] locks a file in place, [Ctrl+R] renames a folder and [Ctrl+N] creates one. Drag-and-drop moves files between folders.
  4. Press [Ctrl+E] to execute. You can review duplicates first, and an audit report is shown when the moves finish.

Press [?] or [F1] for the full list of shortcuts and [Ctrl+Q] to quit. Every shortcut is also listed in Keyboard Shortcuts.

docs.title: From the command line
docs.text:
smart-autosorter scan ~/Downloads            # print the proposed folder tree, move nothing
smart-autosorter scan ~/Downloads --json     # the same plan as JSON, for scripts
smart-autosorter sort ~/Downloads --dry-run  # verify the plan without moving
smart-autosorter sort ~/Downloads            # sort in place
smart-autosorter sort ~/Downloads --dest-dir ~/Sorted

Useful options for sort and scan: - --max-folders N: maximum folders per level (default 12, up to 50). - --strategy: default (keyword clustering), generative (local LLM folder names, needs the ml extra), or the clinical clinical_tmf / clinical_isf strategies. - --conflict-policy skip|rename: what to do when a destination file already exists. - --export-report FILE --report-format html|json: save an audit report of the run. - --preset demo|downloads|documents: use a standard folder instead of naming one. - -q / --quiet and --no-color: less output, and plain text for logs or terminals without color.

docs.title: How Files Are Placed
docs.text:
Each file goes through these steps in order, and the first one that matches decides where it goes: 1. Locked paths you pinned in the TUI. 2. Compliance policies and the sensitivity classifier. Highly sensitive files go to a quarantine folder for review. 3. Keyword rules and rules learned from your past corrections. 4. Extension categories for files whose text isn't extracted (for example Images, Archives, Executables). 5. The folder a file with the same content went to before. 6. Content clustering for everything else.

Clustering groups documents with similar wording and names each folder after its two strongest keywords (for example Finance-Budget). It recurses into large groups to make sub-folders, up to five levels deep. When fewer than three documents are left to cluster at the top level they go to Miscellaneous.

docs.title: Supported File Formats
docs.text: Text is extracted from .txt, .docx, .csv, .xlsx, .xls and .pdf. With the optional ml extra installed, images (.png, .jpg, .jpeg) are read with OCR and audio (.mp3, .wav, .m4a) is transcribed with Whisper (which needs ffmpeg and whisper on your PATH). Every other file type is still sorted, into an extension category folder.

docs.title: Undoing a Run
docs.text:
Every run is recorded as a session that can be rolled back: 

smart-autosorter undo --list           # show recent sessions
smart-autosorter undo --latest         # roll back the most recent run
smart-autosorter undo --session-id ID  # roll back a specific run
In the TUI, [Ctrl+Y] opens the history view.

docs.title: Settings
docs.text: View settings with smart-autosorter config --show, and change one with config --set KEY VALUE. Settings are stored in ~/.autosorter/settings.json; command-line flags override them for a single run. In the TUI, [Ctrl+O] opens the settings dialog.

docs.title: Exclusion list (stop words)
docs.text:
Stop words are common terms (e.g. 'the', 'and', 'for') ignored when analyzing document text. They don't filter file types. 

smart-autosorter config --set STOP_WORDS "word1,word2,word3"

docs.title: Cleaning up empty folders
docs.text:
When enabled, folders left empty after sorting are removed. 

smart-autosorter config --set CLEANUP_EMPTY_FOLDERS true

docs.title: AI consent
docs.text: smart-autosorter config --set AI_CONSENT_GRANTED true

docs.title: Background Folder Monitoring
docs.text:
The daemon watches a folder and sorts new files as they arrive: 

smart-autosorter daemon start ~/Downloads
smart-autosorter daemon status
smart-autosorter daemon stop
pause, resume, health and metrics are also available.

  • Incomplete downloads are ignored. Files ending in .crdownload, .tmp or .download are skipped until they are finished.
  • Bursts are batched. After a file event the daemon waits 0.6 seconds (DEBOUNCE_DELAY) for more changes, and never more than 5 seconds (MAX_DEBOUNCE_DELAY) during a continuous stream of writes.

docs.title: Offline Mode
docs.text: If you decline the model download, are offline during setup, or the model is missing, the app runs without the embedding model: - Documents are still clustered by content, using TF-IDF keyword vectors instead of sentence embeddings. Groupings can be a little less precise for documents that use different words for the same topic. - No network connections are made for the model.

docs.title: Privacy
docs.text: All document processing happens on your machine, and local databases are encrypted. The app's only network traffic is the optional model download and a security-advisory check for that model. See the Privacy Policy (PRIVACY.md in the repository) for details.

docs.title: File contents never leave the machine
docs.text: Sortify extracts, classifies, clusters and names files entirely on the user's machine. The only outbound traffic is fetching model weights from Hugging Face (checked against app/core/hashes_registry.py) and the security-advisory lookup; sandboxed worker threads have socket.connect patched to block anything else (app/core/shared_registry.py), and the offline bundle lets the ML features run with no network at all. We chose this over hosted OCR/LLM APIs because users sort documents (clinical trial files, finances, PHI) that they cannot send to a third party.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• A new feature that needs a model ships the model in the offline bundle or downloads it with a pinned hash. A feature that calls a hosted API with file content contradicts this ADR.
  • network_rules.json only feeds generated docs; it is not the enforcement point.

docs.title: Extracted text and vectors are encrypted at rest with one per-database key
docs.text: Every database that holds extracted text is opened through SQLCipher (app/core/db_conn.py exposes the sqlcipher3 driver as its own sqlite3 handle; sys.modules["sqlite3"] stays the standard library's), and the text and vector columns are additionally Fernet-encrypted (app/core/crypto.py). Both layers use the same key, looked up from the OS keyring first and a 0600 key file second. We accepted the cost (a native SQLCipher dependency, slower queries, key-migration code) because the extracted text is a plain-text copy of the user's sensitive documents.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• New stores of file content go through resolve_db_crypto(db_path); a plain sqlite3.connect or an unencrypted cache file contradicts this ADR.
  • When SQLCipher fails to import, opening a store raises a clear error instead of falling back to the standard library sqlite3 (#711).

docs.title: All database writes go through one writer thread
docs.text: DBWorker (app/core/db_worker.py) is the only thread that writes to a session database: callers enqueue write sessions, it runs each inside BEGIN IMMEDIATE, and readers use per-thread WAL connections. We chose a single serialised writer over a connection pool because SQLite allows one writer at a time, and extraction and moves run on many worker threads that would otherwise fail with database is locked under load.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Code that writes from a worker thread submits the write to DBWorker; opening its own write connection reintroduces lock contention.
  • Long-running work does not happen inside a write session, because it blocks every other writer.

docs.title: Clustering runs in a spawned subprocess on an encrypted payload
docs.text: The default strategy (RecursiveKMeansStrategy in app/core/analyzer_strategies.py) vectorises text with TF-IDF, or ONNX sentence embeddings when a model is present, and clusters with MiniBatchKMeans, recursing until MAX_DEPTH (default 5). It runs in a multiprocessing "spawn" child that receives the documents as an encrypted payload. We chose MiniBatchKMeans over topic models such as NMF or LDA because it clusters large folders quickly with bounded memory and needs no topic count tuning beyond max_folders, and we isolate it in a spawned process so a native-library crash or memory blow-up in scikit-learn/ONNX cannot take down the TUI or the daemon, and so plaintext never crosses the process boundary.

docs.title: Considered options
docs.text:
• NMF topic modelling. Earlier versions of the docs described it; the code no longer uses it.
  • Running in a thread. Rejected: a crash or memory spike in native code would kill the host process.

docs.title: A move never destroys bytes it has not verified exist elsewhere
docs.text:
Every file mutation a sort makes goes through app/core/resilient_file_ops.py, and each one obeys a single rule: Sortify deletes or replaces a file only after it has proved that the same bytes are durable somewhere the ledger knows about. Concretely:

  1. No-replace publish. A file or folder reaches its target path through a rename that fails atomically if the target exists: renameat2(RENAME_NOREPLACE) on Linux and renamex_np(RENAME_EXCL) on macOS, and os.rename on Windows, which never replaces. Where the filesystem lacks the native call, files fall back to os.link(src, dst) then os.unlink(src), and folders to an exclusive mkdir reservation. Only filesystems with neither (EPERM/ENOTSUP/EMLINK from link, as on FAT/exFAT) fall back to check-then-rename under a process-wide lock. The copy fallback runs only on EXDEV, never on any OSError.
  2. Verified cross-volume copy. Copy to a staging file in the target folder, fsync the file and its folder, compare a content hash with the source, publish the stage with the same no-replace primitive, and only then remove the source.
  3. Overwrite displaces, it does not delete. The overwrite conflict policy first moves the existing target into the session's backup folder, recorded in the ledger, and undo restores it. The backup is purged with the session's history, not at move time.
  4. Rollback waits. When a move fails, the mover cancels pending futures and waits for running ones before rollback starts, and rollback replays the ledger for the real session id. With no session id it stops and reports instead of unwinding a random one.
  5. Reconciliation checks hashes. Ledger reconciliation removes a file at a destination only when its hash matches the file_hash the ledger recorded before the move; otherwise it leaves both files and reports a conflict.

We chose this because the five highest risks in the codebase today are all ways the current mover can lose a user's file: atomic_move_non_clobber checks lexists then calls os.rename, which replaces silently on POSIX, and treats any OSError as a cue to copy; overwrite calls resilient_remove(dest) before the move that might fail; cross-volume moves compare only sizes; fut.result() raises on the first failure while the rest of the chunk keeps moving and unwind_session starts underneath it; and reconciliation deletes the destination when both paths exist. Sortify's whole promise is that a sort can be undone, so one irreversible loss outweighs any speed the shortcuts buy.

docs.title: Implementation
docs.text: Points 1, 2 and the wait in point 4 are in #757 and the stacked mover fixes. Still open: point 3 (#766), refusing to sort without a snapshot or session in point 4 (#767), and point 5 (#768).

docs.title: Considered options
docs.text:
• Keep check-then-rename and narrow the window. Rejected: no amount of re-checking closes a TOCTOU race; only an operation that fails atomically does.
  • link + unlink only. Standard library and no foreign calls, but it does not cover folders or symlinks, which the mover does move (junctions and links), it leaves the file with two names for a moment, and it fails outright on FAT/exFAT, which are common on USB drives. We kept it as the first fallback rather than the primary path.
  • Drop the overwrite policy. Simplest and safest, and CONTEXT.md already lists only skip and rename. Rejected for now because app/config.py accepts overwrite and users may rely on it; displacing to a backup keeps it while making it undoable.
  • Size check plus fsync, no hash. Cheaper, but a truncated or corrupted copy of the same size passes. Hashing only runs on the cross-volume path, which is already I/O-bound by the copy.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• The native rename needs per-OS ctypes calls and a support check, and every path below it needs its own tests. The tests in #757 cover each fallback.
  • On the link fallback the file briefly has two names. A crash there leaves a duplicate, never a loss; reconciliation sees two paths with matching hashes and removes the source.
  • The lock-based fallback only protects against Sortify's own workers, not other programs writing into the same folder. That residual race is accepted for filesystems without hard links.
  • Cross-volume moves get slower by one read of the copy. Same-volume moves cost the same as today.
  • Displaced files from overwrite use disk space until their session's history is purged.
  • mover.py and ledger.py stop calling resilient_remove on user files directly. scripts/validate_architecture.py can enforce that only resilient_file_ops deletes user files.
  • Testing this needs a filesystem seam: inject the file operations into resilient_file_ops so tests can fail link, fsync or the hash at each step. That replaces the unittest.mock branches in resilient_move and _process_move_item rather than adding new ones.

docs.title: One move ledger, and undo replays it
docs.text:
Every move a sort makes is recorded in one append-only moves table, and undo, rollback and crash reconciliation all work by replaying that table. Nothing else records moves. Each row holds session_id, seq, src, dst, src_sha256, size, displaced (where an existing file at dst was moved aside to, per ADR 0005) and state, which goes intent → done → verified, or failed. The mover writes intent through DBWorker (ADR 0003) and commits it before it touches the filesystem, then updates the row after the move.

Undo walks a session's verified and done rows backwards. For each one it moves the file back only if the file at dst still has src_sha256 and src is free; otherwise it reports a conflict and leaves both files. Undo never deletes a file it did not create. Rollback is the same undo, started only after every worker in the sort has stopped. Reconciliation on start-up resolves each intent row by finding which path holds the hash.

We chose this because moves are recorded in three places today (transaction_ledger in the main database and again in a sidecar transaction_ledger.db with a different schema, history.db's step_ledger, plus rollback_journal.json), and they can disagree after a crash (#714). Undo instead restores from a pre-sort snapshot of the folder and deletes what the snapshot lacks, which is how it has destroyed hidden files and files created after the sort (#713). A ledger of what Sortify itself did can only ever reverse Sortify's own actions.

docs.title: Considered options
docs.text:
• Keep the snapshot and fix its edge cases. Rejected: a snapshot describes the folder, not Sortify's actions, so restoring it has to decide what to do with every file that changed for any reason. Each fix (#713, #715, #767) narrows the damage without removing the cause.
  • Keep the three ledgers and add a consistency check. Rejected: it keeps three writers to keep in step, and the check would need the same replay logic anyway.
  • Event sourcing for the whole session store. More than this needs. Moves are the only state that must be replayable.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• _rollback_from_snapshot_internal (about 790 lines), the snapshot tables in history.db and rollback_journal.json go away, and so does the test-only _execute_moves_recursive.
  • Sessions written before the change still have only the old ledgers. They need a one-time import into moves, or a read-only legacy undo that is retired after a release or two.
  • One extra committed write per move. DBWorker batches them, and per ADR 0003 no file I/O happens inside the write.
  • The ledger, undo and quarantine CLIs and the TUI history screen read the same table, so they agree with what the sort did.

docs.title: One sort pipeline, built in one place, with layers enforced in CI
docs.text:
A sort runs through one SortPipeline service in app/core, and every front end calls it instead of wiring the steps itself. It has three methods: plan(folders, options) -> Plan, execute(plan) -> SortResult and undo(session_id) -> SortResult. The pipeline owns the order of steps (discover, extract, route and cluster, verify, move), the session, and a per-folder lock file, so two sorts can never run on one folder. SortResult lists what was moved, skipped, quarantined and failed, with reasons, and every front end renders it the same way.

One composition root builds the store, key provider, settings, plugin registry and pipeline. The CLI, TUI, Drop Zone, daemon and demo receive a pipeline and never construct a Database, DBWorker or history manager themselves. CLI flags are an in-memory overlay passed to plan; only config --set and the settings screen save settings. Tests build the same graph with fakes.

Imports point one way: app.main, app.cli and app.ui may import app.core, never the reverse, and plugins reach core only through the registry. scripts/validate_architecture.py fails a PR when app.core imports app.main, app.cli or app.ui, or when a front end imports a store module (db, db_worker, history, ledger) directly (#707).

We chose this because the scan, extract, fit, plan and move sequence is copied about ten times across main.py, tui.py, demo.py, daemon.py and session.py (#708), and each copy wires its own database and history paths (#709). The copies drift: the TUI's Ctrl+S scan never extracts text (#754), the daemon runs blocking sort work on its event loop (#717), Drop Zone and the daemon skip the plan preview the CLI shows, and one-off CLI flags get saved permanently (#735). Since bots write most changes and copy whatever the code already does, the boundary has to be a check, not a convention.

docs.title: Considered options
docs.text:
• A shared helper function per step, called by each front end. Less churn, but every front end still decides the order and the error handling, which is exactly what has drifted.
  • One run_sort() function with flags. Simpler than a service, but the TUI needs to show the plan and ask before moving, and the daemon needs to queue work. Separate plan and execute serve both, and run_sort is just execute(plan(...)).
  • Dependency-injection framework. Not needed: one hand-written function that builds the graph is enough at this size and is easier for an agent to read.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Drop Zone and the daemon get the same preview and simulation as the CLI, and the daemon becomes a thin asyncio front end that queues work for the pipeline (#717).
  • The production unittest.mock and PYTEST_CURRENT_TEST branches (#720) can go, because tests inject fakes through the composition root instead.
  • Plugins add routers, strategies and quarantine hooks through one registry, so core stops naming clinical_compliance (#723).
  • Splitting tui.py (#710) gets easier: screens call the pipeline instead of holding sort logic.
  • Front ends lose the freedom to reorder steps. A new need, such as a scan-only mode, becomes a pipeline option rather than another copy.

docs.title: One app store, versioned by numbered migrations
docs.text:
Sortify keeps its state in one encrypted SQLite store under ~/.autosorter/, not in per-session databases in the system temp folder. Sessions are rows in that store, alongside documents, vectors, moves (ADR 0006), quarantine_records and settings_audit. Every connection runs PRAGMA foreign_keys=ON, so deleting a document cascades to its vectors.

The schema has one version, held in PRAGMA user_version. Changes are numbered migration functions in one module (0001_initial, 0002_…), each run once, in order, inside a transaction, and never edited after release. Opening a store newer than the code refuses with a clear message rather than guessing. Extraction status is a column on documents, not a [STATUS:FAILED] string stored as the document text, so failed extractions can be retried when the extractor changes.

We chose this because schema changes today are ad hoc in four modules (#712): db.py checks user_version for some changes and then runs ALTER TABLE documents ADD COLUMN rating inside try/except: pass on every open, and history.py does the same for ten snapshot_files columns. Errors other than "column exists" are swallowed with them. Foreign keys are never enabled, so ON DELETE CASCADE on document_vectors does nothing and deletes leave encrypted vectors behind. Per-session databases in the temp folder mean undo history can vanish on reboot, and the ledger and quarantine CLIs read a different database from the one sorts write to.

docs.title: Considered options
docs.text:
• Alembic. Mature, but it brings SQLAlchemy, its own config and its own history table, and it has to be taught about SQLCipher keys. A dozen small functions and user_version cover a single-user embedded store.
  • Keep per-session databases, add migrations to each. Keeps cleanup as deleting a folder, but every session database needs migrating, and queries across sessions (history, ledger, quarantine) still have to open many files.
  • Keep try/ALTER/except. Rejected: it can't express anything but adding a column, it hides real errors, and it runs on every open.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Undo history survives a reboot, and every CLI and screen sees the same sessions.
  • One key per store, instead of a keyring entry per session database.
  • The store grows over time, so it needs a retention setting and a purge command. Deleting a session becomes a DELETE plus a VACUUM, not rm -r.
  • Existing session databases need a one-time import, done by the first migration and shared with the ledger import in ADR 0006.
  • Enabling foreign keys can make existing orphan rows fail checks, so the first migration deletes orphans before turning the pragma on.
  • A failing migration rolls back and leaves the store at its previous version, so a bad release cannot half-upgrade it.

docs.title: Auto-merge decides by path tier, and data-safety code always needs a human
docs.text:
Bots write most of Sortify's changes, and scripts/auto_merge_controller.py merges the ones scripts/classify_pr.py calls low-risk. Every changed path falls into one of three tiers, and the PR takes the strictest tier any of its files hits:

  1. Docs (docs/, README.md, mkdocs.yml): auto-merge once Required CI passes on the current head.
  2. Code and tests: auto-merge only with the automerge label applied by a maintainer (a person with write access, not a bot), within the size limits, with Required CI green. Tests stay here rather than with docs, because a bot that deletes or weakens a failing test would otherwise merge unreviewed.
  3. Protected paths: never auto-merged; the owner must approve. These are the security paths already listed (.github/, SECURITY.md, PRIVACY.md, app/config.py, app/core/crypto.py, scripts/, the PyInstaller spec, network_rules.json, .gitleaks.toml, dependency manifests outside Dependabot) plus every module that can lose a user's file: app/core/mover.py, resilient_file_ops.py, ledger.py, history.py, session.py, db.py, db_conn.py, db_worker.py and quarantine_interceptor.py, and snapshot baselines.

PROTECTED_PATHS in scripts/classify_pr.py is the one list of protected paths, written in CODEOWNERS syntax. .github/CODEOWNERS has to list every entry, and tests/test_risk_classifier.py fails when the two disagree, so GitHub's code-owner review and the controller enforce the same boundary. A Dependabot bump counts as major from the version numbers in its title (a new first component, or a new second one under 0.x); titles without one from A to B, such as grouped updates, count as major. Only the exact dependabot[bot] login counts as Dependabot; a dependencies label does not.

We chose this because the gate today leaves the code that matters most open. The classifier protects mover.py, history.py and session.py, but not resilient_file_ops.py, ledger.py or the db* modules, which is where the move and undo bugs fixed in #757 to #768 lived. CODEOWNERS and SENSITIVE_PATHS are separate lists that already differ (CODEOWNERS lacks scripts/ and the spec file). The automerge opt-in is a label the PR's own author can add. And "major" dependency bumps are detected by searching the PR title for "major" or "breaking", which Dependabot titles don't contain.

docs.title: Considered options
docs.text:
• Turn auto-merge off. Safest, but the owner merges in bulk today and the bots open about 15 PRs a day; without a gate, the review load lands on one person and gets skipped.
  • Require human review on everything except docs. Simple, but it sends routine UI and test changes to the same queue as mover changes, so the queue stops being read.
  • Gate on test coverage of the changed lines instead of paths. Better in principle, but the coverage gate is a no-op today (#738), and coverage doesn't show whether a test would catch data loss.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• PRs touching the protected data-safety modules wait for the owner even when CI is green. That is the intent until the property test from the system design (random plans against a folder of unrelated and hidden files, killed at random points, then reconciled and undone, with every original file byte-identical) runs in Required CI. After that, revisit whether db* can drop to tier 2.
  • The label check costs two API calls per labelled PR (issue events, then the labeller's permission) and fails closed: if either call fails, the label is ignored.
  • Adding a protected path means editing PROTECTED_PATHS and CODEOWNERS together, which the test enforces.
  • The classify-pr.yml workflow still guesses major bumps from the title when it labels a PR. Its labels only pre-filter: the controller re-classifies with this logic before merging, so the gate holds, but the labels can say automerge:eligible for a PR the controller will refuse.
  • Branch protection must require code-owner review for this to hold when someone merges by hand. That setting can't be seen from the repository, so it has to be confirmed in GitHub's settings.

docs.title: 1. Context & Overview
docs.text: This notebook demonstrates how the Smart AutoSorter AI Pro's core machine learning engine works under the hood. The system utilizes an IncrementalAnalyzer that processes documents and automatically clusters them into semantic themes. This process allows developers and integration engineers to understand document themes without manual categorization.

docs.title: 2. Parameter Explanations & Expectations
docs.text: The IncrementalAnalyzer class requires several parameters to govern its behavior and state: - max_folders (int): The most folders the analyzer creates at each level of the tree. Each level gets min(max_folders, documents // 2) clusters, at least 2. In the app this comes from the MAX_FOLDERS setting (default 12, allowed 1 to 50). - stop_words (set): A set of common words (e.g., 'the', 'and', 'for') that are filtered out during tokenization and TF-IDF calculation to ensure meaningful clustering. - db (Database): An active Database instance. The analyzer is stateful and stores TF-IDF vocabularies, document mappings, and other metadata inside this SQLite-backed database. - strategy_name (str): Specifies the clustering strategy. 'default' is the fully offline strategy: recursive KMeans with folders named from TF-IDF keywords, and what the app uses unless AI-assisted naming is on. 'generative' names folders with a local LLM. If you omit the argument the constructor uses 'generative', so pass 'default' explicitly as this tutorial does. - model_path (str/None): The path to the ONNX embedding model. Passing None forces TF-IDF keyword vectors, with no model loading at all. Omitting the argument is different: the analyzer then looks for a model in the offline bundle or the app's data folder and uses it if one is installed.

docs.title: Expected Inputs:
docs.text:
• Base Directory (base_dir): The root directory being analyzed.
  • Corpus (new_corpus): A dictionary mapping file relative paths to their extracted text content (or dictionaries with 'text' and 'hash' keys).

docs.title: Expected Outputs:
docs.text: • Sorting Plan: A nested dictionary representation of the proposed directory structure containing files mapped to destination paths and categories based on mathematical clustering profiles.

docs.title: Stateful Clustering Architecture
docs.text:
import json
import tempfile
from pathlib import Path

from app.core.analyzer import IncrementalAnalyzer
from app.core.db import Database
from app.core.db_conn import clear_connection_cache

# Core imports from Smart AutoSorter AI Pro
from app.core.db_worker import DBWorker

docs.title: 3. Sandboxing & Safe Database Initialization
docs.text:
To prevent modifying any live user data, we set up a temporary directory to serve as our isolated sandbox. All document processing and database writes will occur within this folder.

# Create an isolated sandbox environment
sandbox_dir = tempfile.TemporaryDirectory()
base_dir = sandbox_dir.name
print(f"[*] Sandbox directory initialized safely at: {base_dir}")

# Instantiate the background database worker and local SQLite DB
db_worker = DBWorker()
db_path = Path(base_dir) / "sandbox_autosorter.db"
db = Database(db_path, db_worker)
print(f"[+] Sandbox Database initialized successfully at: {db_path}")

docs.title: 4. Analyzer Initialization
docs.text:
Now, we initialize our stateful IncrementalAnalyzer. We'll configure it with a maximum limit of 3 folders, a clean set of stop words, and use the 'default' KMeans clustering strategy.

# Stop words to filter out noise words during clustering
stop_words = {
    "the",
    "and",
    "for",
    "this",
    "that",
    "with",
    "from",
    "your",
    "will",
    "are",
    "not",
    "can",
}

analyzer = IncrementalAnalyzer(
    max_folders=3,
    stop_words=stop_words,
    db=db,
    strategy_name="default",
    model_path=None,  # Fallback to local keyword-based recursive KMeans strategy
)
print("[+] Stateful IncrementalAnalyzer successfully initialized!")

docs.title: 5. Feeding Documents (Incremental Training)
docs.text:
We define a diverse sample corpus spanning three distinct themes: Finance, Technology, and Healthcare. We train the analyzer incrementally by feeding chunks using partial_fit.

sample_corpus = {
    "invoice_1042.txt": "invoice billing statement payment wire transfer balance sheet finance department banking profit revenue expense ledger audit audit",
    "quarterly_report.txt": "finance banking revenue quarterly profits balance sheet asset liability stock market investment ledger statement account billing payment",
    "neural_net_notes.txt": "machine learning artificial intelligence deep learning algorithms computer science software python neural networks model train GPU CPU programming git",
    "api_integration.txt": "software engineering python computer science developers api git source code debug program system architecture database query server",
    "clinical_trial_a.txt": "medical patient medicine health clinical trial cardiology pharmaceutical dosage diagnosis therapy disease doctor physician hospital treatment",
    "patient_health_summary.txt": "health patient medical clinic diagnosis doctor medicine therapy hospital pharmaceutical cardiology trial disease treatment blood pressure dosage",
}

print("[*] Training the stateful analyzer on the sample corpus...")
analyzer.partial_fit(base_dir, sample_corpus)
print("[+] Partial fit complete. All documents ingested and TF-IDF tables populated.")

docs.title: 6. Generating the Sorting Plan
docs.text:
With the analyzer trained, we generate a sorting plan mapping files to proposed directory folders. The analyzer automatically inspects the themes of our files and clusters them accordingly.

print("[*] Generating sorting plan based on semantic similarities...")
plan = analyzer.generate_sorting_plan(base_dir)

print("\n[+] Proposed Sorting Plan:")
print(json.dumps(plan, indent=2))

docs.title: 7. Clean Resource Teardown
docs.text:
Lastly, we ensure all background workers and temporary resources are terminated and cleaned up properly.

print("[*] Terminating analyzer and database background threads...")
analyzer.terminate()
db_worker.stop()
clear_connection_cache(only_current_and_inactive=False)
sandbox_dir.cleanup()
print("[+] Sandbox environment cleaned up successfully. Bye!")

docs.title: Multi-Format Text Extraction & Local Session Management
1. Context & Overview
docs.text: This notebook demonstrates the document ingestion layer of Smart AutoSorter AI Pro. We will explore: 1. Local Session Management: Initializing and managing the lifespan of an application run via AppSession. 2. Multi-Format Text Extraction: Writing programmatically supported formats (.txt, .csv, .docx, .xlsx) to disk and extracting their text content safely. 3. Database Inspection: Inspecting the internal SQLite databases to verify that file text, hashes, and schemas are correctly registered in the system's storage layer.

docs.title: Extraction Pipeline Flow
docs.text:
import csv
import os
import tempfile

# Install helpers/libraries for office formats
import docx
import openpyxl

# Core Smart AutoSorter imports
from app.config import Settings
from app.core.db_conn import clear_connection_cache, get_db_connection
from app.core.extractor import build_corpus_generator
from app.core.session import AppSession

docs.title: 2. Sandbox Setup & Generating Sample Documents
docs.text:
To guarantee isolated execution, we create a temporary directory and generate files across various supported formats.

# Set up a secure, isolated temporary workspace
sandbox_dir = tempfile.TemporaryDirectory()
base_dir = sandbox_dir.name
print(f"[*] Safe base workspace directory: {base_dir}")

# 1. Create a plain text (.txt) file
txt_path = os.path.join(base_dir, "sample_notes.txt")
with open(txt_path, "w", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    f.write(
        "Software development notes. Python programming, unit tests, and continuous integration pipelines."
    )

# 2. Create a CSV (.csv) spreadsheet file
csv_path = os.path.join(base_dir, "sample_spreadsheet.csv")
with open(csv_path, "w", encoding="utf-8", newline="") as f:
    writer = csv.writer(f)
    writer.writerow(["Item", "Amount", "Department"])
    writer.writerow(["Servers", "25000", "Infrastructure"])
    writer.writerow(["Monitors", "12000", "Hardware"])

# 3. Create a Microsoft Word (.docx) file
docx_path = os.path.join(base_dir, "sample_doc.docx")
doc = docx.Document()
doc.add_heading("Project Specification", level=1)
doc.add_paragraph(
    "This document details clinical trial results, healthcare diagnostics, and medical treatments."
)
doc.save(docx_path)

# 4. Create an Excel (.xlsx) workbook file
xlsx_path = os.path.join(base_dir, "sample_ledger.xlsx")
wb = openpyxl.Workbook()
ws = wb.active
ws.title = "Financial Overview"
ws["A1"] = "Quarterly Budget Report"
ws["A2"] = "Total Investment Assets and Balance Sheets"
ws["B2"] = 750000
wb.save(xlsx_path)

files_created = [
    os.path.basename(p) for p in [txt_path, csv_path, docx_path, xlsx_path]
]
print(f"[+] Generated {len(files_created)} sample multi-format files: {files_created}")

docs.title: 3. Session Initialization & Core Ingestion Pipeline
docs.text:
We now instantiate our custom AppSession utilizing explicit Settings. We then trigger the synchronous build_corpus_generator to run text extraction across all the generated formats.

# Initialize settings with AI consent disabled for deterministic, lightweight extraction
settings = Settings(AI_CONSENT_GRANTED=False, MAX_FOLDERS=5)

# Initialize AppSession
session = AppSession(settings=settings, base_dir=base_dir)
print(f"[+] AppSession initialized! ID: {session.session_id}")
print(f"[*] App store holding documents and history: {session.store.path}")


def progress_callback():
    """Progress callback function for text extraction."""
    print("    -> Extracting file...")


# Execute synchronous extraction of text payload and hashing from sample documents
generator = build_corpus_generator(
    base_dir=base_dir,
    items_to_sort=files_created,
    progress_callback=progress_callback,
    max_workers=2,
    db=session.db,
    chunk_size=10,
    sequential=True,
    settings=settings,
)

extracted_chunks = list(generator)
print(f"\n[+] Ingestion complete! Processed {len(extracted_chunks)} chunks.")

docs.title: 4. Database Inspection via SQL
docs.text:
We connect directly to the app store (sortify.db), the one SQLite database every session writes to, to inspect the tables. This allows developers to audit the exact extracted text strings and calculated unique file hashes stored persistently.

db_file = session.store.path
print(f"[*] Connecting to the app store: {db_file}")

conn = get_db_connection(str(db_file))
cursor = conn.cursor()

# 1. Fetch tables schema list
cursor.execute("SELECT name FROM sqlite_master WHERE type='table';")
tables = cursor.fetchall()
print(f"[+] Database Tables present: {[t[0] for t in tables]}")

# 2. Query documents table
cursor.execute("SELECT filepath, file_hash, extracted_text FROM documents;")
records = cursor.fetchall()

print("\n--- Persisted Documents & Extracted Content ---")
for filepath, f_hash, text in records:
    text_str = session.db.crypto.decrypt_text(text) if isinstance(text, bytes) else text
    truncated_text = text_str[:100] + "..." if len(text_str) > 100 else text_str
    print(f"File: {filepath}")
    print(f"  Hash: {f_hash}")
    print(f"  Text preview: {truncated_text}")
    print("-" * 45)

conn.close()

docs.title: 5. Clean Resource Teardown
docs.text:
Finally, close the session to release file locks on databases, and safely delete the temporary sandbox.

print("[*] Closing session and cleaning up directories...")
session.close()
clear_connection_cache(only_current_and_inactive=False)
sandbox_dir.cleanup()
print("[+] Environment cleaned up. Extraction workflow complete!")

docs.title: Virtual Sorting Verification & Safe Simulation Testing
1. Context & Overview
docs.text:
Before performing physical move/rename operations on a user's filesystem, Smart AutoSorter AI Pro executes a proactive, in-memory dry run verification using the VerificationEngine.

This safety check guarantees: 1. No dynamic path collisions: Preventing multiple source files from overwriting each other if they are assigned to the same target path. 2. No invalid/long paths: Detecting and warning if any generated destination paths violate the standard operating system character limits (e.g. 260 character limit on Windows). 3. Safe Simulation: Performing validation entirely in memory without actually writing, copying, or deleting any files on disk.

docs.title: Virtual Verification Pipeline Flow
docs.text:
import json
import os
import tempfile

# Core Smart AutoSorter imports
from app.core.verifier import VerificationEngine

docs.title: 2. Sandbox Setup
docs.text:
We'll instantiate a clean sandbox directory to mock our local filesystem base path.

# Setup mock workspace
sandbox_dir = tempfile.TemporaryDirectory()
base_dir = os.path.normpath(sandbox_dir.name)
print(f"[*] Safe mock workspace base dir: {base_dir}")

docs.title: 3. Scenario 1: Normal Sorting Operations (Successful Validation)
docs.text:
We configure a clean sorting plan with non-conflicting destinations. Folders are plain nested dictionaries, as the analyzer produces them, and files are nodes with "__type__": "file". (A node with "__type__": "directory" means "move this whole folder as one unit", so the verifier does not look inside it.) A rename (target_filename different from the source name) only passes once the user has confirmed it, so the plan marks it confirmed. The VerificationEngine simulates the moves and should report success.

normal_plan = {
    "document_A.txt": {
        "__type__": "file",
        "relative_source": "document_A.txt",
        "target_filename": "document_A.txt",
    },
    "Finance": {
        "document_B.txt": {
            "__type__": "file",
            "relative_source": "document_B.txt",
            "target_filename": "renamed_B.txt",
            "confirmed": True,  # the user approved this rename
        },
    },
}

print("[*] Verifying normal sorting plan integrity...")
result = VerificationEngine.verify_plan_integrity(base_dir, normal_plan)

print("\n[+] Verification Result:")
print(f"  Success: {result['success']}")
print(f"  Warnings: {result['warnings']}")
print(f"  Collisions: {result['collisions']}")
assert result["success"] and not result["collisions"]

docs.title: 4. Scenario 2: Dynamic Path Collision Detection
docs.text:
Now, let's intentionally introduce a collision where two separate source files are directed to the same destination target file. The VerificationEngine must proactively detect this and mark the plan verification as unsuccessful.

colliding_plan = {
    "Finance": {
        "invoice_1.txt": {
            "__type__": "file",
            "relative_source": "invoice_1.txt",
            "target_filename": "clashing_name.txt",
        },
        "receipt_9.txt": {
            "__type__": "file",
            "relative_source": "receipt_9.txt",
            "target_filename": "clashing_name.txt",  # Collision!
        },
    }
}

print("[*] Verifying colliding plan integrity...")
result = VerificationEngine.verify_plan_integrity(base_dir, colliding_plan)

print("\n[-] Verification Result:")
print(f"  Success: {result['success']}")
print(f"  Collisions: {json.dumps(result['collisions'], indent=2)}")
print(f"  Warnings: {result['warnings']}")
assert not result["success"]
assert result["collisions"][0]["type"] == "duplicate_target"

Besides the collision, the warnings also flag both renames as lacking user confirmation, because neither node sets confirmed.

docs.title: 5. Scenario 3: Windows Path Length Warnings Limit Detection
docs.text:
Destinations of 260 characters or more fail verification on every OS, because Windows can't open them by default. We'll simulate a plan containing a filename with 250 characters, which pushes the full destination path over the limit.

long_filename = "x" * 250 + ".txt"
long_path_plan = {
    "short_file.txt": {
        "__type__": "file",
        "relative_source": "short_file.txt",
        "target_filename": long_filename,
    }
}

print("[*] Verifying long-path plan integrity...")
result = VerificationEngine.verify_plan_integrity(base_dir, long_path_plan)

print("\n[-] Verification Result:")
print(f"  Success: {result['success']}")
print(f"  Long Paths Found: {len(result['long_paths'])}")
if result["long_paths"]:
    print(f"  Example long path truncated: {result['long_paths'][0]['path'][:80]}...")
print(f"  Warnings: {result['warnings']}")
assert not result["success"] and len(result["long_paths"]) == 1

docs.title: 6. Safe Workspace Cleanup
docs.text:
Clean up the temporary sandbox workspace safely.

print("[*] Cleaning up mock sandbox base directory...")
sandbox_dir.cleanup()
print("[+] Workspace deleted. Verification simulation finalized safely!")
